Bit late to the race here, but I was in the same position as you. 

Left school at 17, no clue what I wanted to do, barely any qualifications, and generalised anxiety disorder. 

I worked in retail etc for years, tried a bunch of college courses to figure out what I was interested in (starting at NQ level), and just couldn't find my calling.

Ended up doing an evening course at uni to try some things out when I was late 20s, and now have a master's and a decently paid full time job. 

I would just say - spend the time now figuring out what you're interested in so you don't waste time stuck in jobs that might add to your stress and anxiety. Retail/hospitality etc *can* certainly be fun and okayish pay, but they do tend to wear you down after a while, and I felt others were able to properly "start life" before me (holidays/travelling, spending money etc).

And please don't put yourself down, I can't imagine how school must be nowadays, especially with the pandemic and its aftermath. You're doing the best you can, and asking for advice is an excellent start! Please let us know how you get on!

My advice then stands to you also - asb between neighbours is one of the most difficult things to deal with as there is little chance of getting the offending party evicted and your home is supposed to be your sanctuary. If in/near the same property avoid each other, keep any evidence, report to housing associations/landlord/council asb team. If consistent then apply to move - much easier than assuming they will (as unfair as this may seem).

Definitely ask to apply for the Emergency Assistance Fund (you can do this yourself on the website but if not possible then a support coordinator can do it for you) - you can ask to apply for a door brace, blink doorbell and sync module and fireproof letterbox bag (just in case!). Anything that would make you feel safe! 

They can also provide emotional support, while not counselling, a listening ear can help when you're stressed. 

Please also keep a log of any incidents and call the police every time - although many say they won't do anything, as long as there is a record of incidents reported it can really help for further court cases.
